855.title: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
855.hook: the Prophet's host in Medina, who, tradition says, was buried at the walls of Constantinople
855.howItsDone: Muslims tell Abu Ayyub's story from Sahih Muslim, where he hosts the Prophet in Medina, and remember him as a model of hospitality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khabbab, the blacksmith who would not sell his faith for a debt. Your line was: the blacksmith endured. What small discomfort did you carry for someone else? Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Middle of the night, in a two-story house in Medina. A man wakes up and can't get back to sleep, because of where he's lying. Downstairs, right under his floor, his guest is sleeping. And the guest is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Every step this man and his wife take up here, every shuffle, is over the Prophet's head. He gets up, and the two of them move into a corner, and stay there till morning. Today: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and what it looks like to take a guest seriously.
screen: `MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.` → `THE GUEST IS DOWNSTAIRS.` → `THEY MOVE INTO A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim tells it from Abu Ayyub himself. When the Prophet came to Medina, he stayed in Abu Ayyub's house. The Prophet chose the lower floor, and Abu Ayyub and his family lived above. After that sleepless night, Abu Ayyub went to him. The Prophet explained: the lower floor is easier for me. Abu Ayyub answered: I will not go up onto a roof that you are under. So the Prophet moved upstairs, and his host moved down. Then there's the food. Abu Ayyub would send up meals, and when the dish came back, he would ask where the Prophet's fingers had been, and eat from that spot. One day the dish came back untouched. It had garlic in it. Abu Ayyub went up, worried. Is it forbidden? No, the Prophet said, but I don't like it. Then, said Abu Ayyub, I dislike what you dislike. That's hosting with attention: noticing the floor, the plate, the smell of garlic. A good host keeps learning the guest. And then the story jumps forward, a long way. The Sunan of Abu Dawud places Abu Ayyub with a Muslim army at Constantinople, explaining a verse of the Qur'an to the soldiers there. Tradition says he died on that campaign and asked to be buried as close to the city's walls as they could reach. The man who once wouldn't walk over the Prophet's head ended his life far from that house, still on the road. The host.
screen: `THE LOWER FLOOR IS EASIER FOR ME.` · `NOT ON A ROOF THAT YOU ARE UNDER.` · `I DISLIKE WHAT YOU DISLIKE.` · `FAR AWAY, AT CONSTANTINOPLE.` · then, large: `THE HOST.`

segments.voice: The practice: host someone well. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who will be in your space soon. A visiting relative, a friend for coffee, a colleague at your desk, a child coming home from school. Breathe in, and picture them arriving. What would make it easier for them? A chair that's free. A drink they like. Your phone face down. Breathe out, and pick one small thing to prepare. If you pray, you can ask blessing on the people who come through your door. The bell holds the time.
Abu Ayyub. The man of Medina whose house sheltered the Prophet, and who, tradition says, was buried near the walls of Constantinople. Today's word.
Your line: the host. Today, when someone comes to you, notice one thing they like or don't like, and act on it. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
856.hook: the Ansar chief whose death shook the Throne (Bukhari)
856.howItsDone: Muslims remember Sa'd ibn Mu'adh from reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, above all the Prophet's words that the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Ayyub, who moved downstairs so his guest could sleep above. Your line was: the host. What did you notice about a guest today? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

The Throne of the Most Merciful shook. That's the sentence. Jabir ibn Abdullah says he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say it, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it, in a chapter about one man. Not a prophet. Not a king. The chief of a clan in Medina, wounded in battle, who died of the wound. What kind of life gets a sentence like that at its end? Today: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.
screen: `THE THRONE SHOOK.` → `NOT A PROPHET, NOT A KING.` → `WHAT KIND OF LIFE?`

segments.voice: Sa'd was a leader of the Aws, a tribe of Medina, and the early biographies say that when he accepted Islam, his clan followed him. So he wasn't a private believer. He was a chief, with people looking at him. Bukhari shows what that looked like. Sa'd went to Mecca to perform the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, staying with an old friend there. Abu Jahl, a leader of the Prophet's opponents, stopped him at the Kaaba and sneered that he was walking around safely after giving shelter to the Prophet's people. Sa'd didn't lower his voice. If you stop me from this, he said, I'll stop you from something worse: your trade road to Syria, which runs past Medina. A chief speaking as a chief, for the people under his protection. At the battle of the Trench, Sa'd was hit by an arrow in the arm. We met the tent where he was cared for, Rufaydah's tent in the mosque, on an earlier day. In his last days he was also asked to give a judgment in a hard and painful case, one the histories record and readers still wrestle with; that story needs its own day. The wound did not heal, and he died of it. That's when the Prophet said the Throne shook. And Bukhari adds another scene. Someone gave the Prophet a garment of silk, and people kept touching it, amazed at how soft it was. The Prophet said: the handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this. A handkerchief, a small, everyday thing, and still finer than the softest thing in the room. Sa'd held one role, chief of his people, and he held it the same way in Mecca, in battle, and in a tent with a wound that wouldn't close. The throne shook.
screen: `A CHIEF, WITH PEOPLE WATCHING.` · `FACING ABU JAHL AT THE KAABA.` · `AN ARROW AT THE TRENCH.` · `HANDKERCHIEFS FINER THAN SILK.` · then, large: `THE THRONE SHOOK.`

segments.voice: The practice: be sincere in one role. Settle, and breathe. You hold more than one role. Parent, child, friend, worker, neighbor, member of something. Let them pass by, one by one. Then choose one. Breathe in, and ask: in this role, where am I one person in public and another in private? Breathe out, and let one small difference close. Not all of them. One. If you pray, you can ask for sincerity, which Muslims call ikhlas, in that one role. The bell holds the time.
Sa'd. The chief of Medina who stood up to Abu Jahl, was wounded at the Trench, and at whose death, the Prophet said, the Throne shook. Today's word.
Your line: the throne shook. Today, in the one role you chose, act the same way whether anyone is watching or not. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: Uways al-Qarani
857.hook: a man from Yemen who never met the Prophet ﷺ, cared for his mother, and whose prayers were sought
857.tomorrow: The women who asked for a day
857.howItsDone: Muslims retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Umar seeking out Uways and asking for his prayer, and often hold him up as an example of devotion to a parent and of a hidden, humble life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sa'd, the chief of the Ansar. Your line was: the throne shook. In which one role did you try to be sincere? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

Every time a fresh group of fighters arrives in Medina from Yemen, Umar ibn al-Khattab goes out to meet them with the same question. Is Uways ibn Amir among you? Again and again, no. Umar leads the whole community by now, with no shortage of other business. And still he keeps asking after one man, a man he has never seen. Then one day a voice in the crowd says yes. Umar walks up to him and asks his own favor: pray for me. Today: Uways al-Qarani.
screen: `IS UWAYS AMONG YOU?` → `AGAIN AND AGAIN, NO.` → `THEN ONE DAY, YES.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih Muslim, and Umar tells us why he kept asking. He had heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, describe a man who would come with the reinforcements from Yemen: Uways ibn Amir, of the tribe of Murad, then of the clan of Qaran. He had suffered a skin disease and been cured of it, except for one small patch. And he had a mother, and he was devoted to her. Then the Prophet said something remarkable: if this man swore by God, God would make his oath come true. If you meet him, ask him to seek forgiveness for you. So Umar checks every detail, one by one, and Uways confirms them all. Murad, Qaran, the healed skin, the mother. Then Umar, the companion of the Prophet, asks a man who never met the Prophet to pray for him. And Uways does. Why did he never meet him? The hadith only says he had a mother and was dutiful to her. Tradition says that is exactly what kept him in Yemen: she needed him, and he stayed. Hold that part as the tradition's telling, not the hadith's words. Then comes the end of the conversation, which is easy to miss. Umar asks where he is going. Kufa, says Uways. Umar offers to write to the governor there for him. And Uways declines. He says he would rather be among the ordinary people, the ones nobody notices. He had a recommendation from the leader of the believers in his hand, and he let it go. Look at the shape of it. The man whose prayer was sought was the man who did not seek to be seen. In the Prophet's description, the one deed named is not a battle or a speech. It is his care for his mother.
screen: `DESCRIBED BY THE PROPHET.` · `DEVOTED TO HIS MOTHER.` · `UMAR ASKS HIM TO PRAY.` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY UNNOTICED.` · then, large: `HE STAYED WITH HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for a parent today. Let your breath slow down. Bring your mother or father to mind, or whoever raised you. Breathe in, and think of one ordinary thing they need right now. A call. A ride. A meal. Their medicine picked up. Ten minutes of listening without checking your phone. Breathe out, and decide on that one thing. If your parent has died, you can hold them in mind instead, and if you pray, you can ask mercy for them. If the relationship is hard, you can choose something small and safe, or simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Uways al-Qarani. A man of Qaran in Yemen, devoted to his mother, described by the Prophet, and sought out by Umar for his prayer. Today's word.
Your line: he stayed with his mother. Today, do the one thing you chose for a parent, and don't post about it. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: The women who asked for a day
858.hook: women asked the Prophet ﷺ for a day to teach them, and he gave it
858.howItsDone: Muslims cite this report from Sahih al-Bukhari when talking about women's study of the religion, and mosques and communities hold classes and circles for women.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uways al-Qarani, the man from Yemen whose prayer Umar sought. Your line was: he stayed with his mother. What did you do for a parent? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

A complaint, made out loud, to the Prophet himself. The men, a group of women tell the Prophet, have taken all of your time. Every gathering, every lesson, every question answered, the men are there first, crowding in. So the women make a request. Set aside a day for us, just for us, when we can come and learn from you. It's a short scene in Sahih al-Bukhari, a few lines long. But it's the kind of request that can be brushed off with a vague promise. Today: the women who asked for a day.
screen: `THE MEN HAVE TAKEN YOUR TIME.` → `SET ASIDE A DAY FOR US.` → `WHAT WILL HE SAY?`

segments.voice: Bukhari places this report in his book on knowledge, and the narrator is the companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The women come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and they name the problem plainly: the men are taking up your time. They don't ask for a favor. They ask for a day. And the hadith says he promised them one. Then he kept it. He met them on that day, the report says, and he advised them and taught them. Notice what that means. Teaching was not something that happened to women by accident, overheard from the back of a room. When they asked, a time was made for them on purpose, and the Prophet showed up. Then we get a glimpse of what was said. He told them that a woman who loses three of her children will find them a shield for her from the Fire. And one woman, in the middle of the lesson, asks a follow-up question. And two? He says: and two. Pause on that. These are not abstract lessons. The women brought their real lives into the room, including the grief of losing a child, and the teaching met them there. And a woman felt free to interrupt and ask about her own case. That is what a day for learning looks like: a set time, a teacher who arrives, and room for the question you actually have. In the same book on knowledge, Aisha is remembered praising the women of the Ansar, because shyness did not stop them from learning their religion. The request for a day sits in that company.
screen: `THEY NAMED THE PROBLEM.` · `HE PROMISED A DAY, AND KEPT IT.` · `THEY BROUGHT THEIR REAL GRIEF.` · `ROOM FOR THE NEXT QUESTION.` · then, large: `A DAY FOR LEARNING.`

segments.voice: The practice: make time to teach someone. Sit comfortably, and let your breathing even out. Bring to mind a person who has asked you, maybe more than once, to show them something. How to cook a dish. How to read a page of Arabic. How to fix a bike, file a form, pray a prayer. Maybe you said, sure, sometime. Breathe in, and picture their face. Breathe out, and give that sometime a real day and an hour. Then picture yourself actually turning up, and leaving room for their question. The bell holds the time.
Ansar. The helpers of Medina, whose women asked the Prophet for a day of their own, and he gave it and taught them. Today's word.
Your line: a day for learning. Today, put the date in your calendar for the person you'll teach, and tell them. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
859.hook: a companion whose recitation the Prophet ﷺ likened to the pipes of the family of Dawud
859.howItsDone: Muslims value beautiful, careful recitation of the Qur'an (tajwid), and Abu Musa's reported gift comes up when people speak of reciting with a lovely voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ansar women who asked the Prophet for a day of their own. Your line was: a day for learning. Did the person you'll teach get a date? Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Night in Medina. A man is reciting the Qur'an, for no one in particular. He doesn't know that out in the dark, someone has stopped to listen. The next day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells him: if only you had seen me last night, listening to your recitation. Then he adds a compliment. You have been given one of the pipes of the family of Dawud. Today: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a man from Yemen with a voice worth stopping for.
screen: `RECITING AT NIGHT, ALONE.` → `SOMEONE STOPS TO LISTEN.` → `A PIPE OF DAWUD'S FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Start with the compliment. The word in the hadith is mizmar, a reed pipe, a wind instrument. Dawud, the prophet David, is remembered in the Qur'an as one with whom the mountains and the birds joined in praise. So when the Prophet said Abu Musa had a pipe of Dawud's family, he was saying: your voice carries something of that. Muslim and Bukhari both record it. But here's the turn. Abu Musa is also the companion who narrates a very different kind of lesson about voices. On a journey, he reports, the companions were climbing and calling out God is greatest at the top of their lungs. And the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves. You are not calling on someone deaf or absent, he said. You are calling on One who hears, and who is near. Put those two reports side by side. The sweet voice was heard at night, unplanned, not on a stage. And the loud voices were gently quieted. Beauty in recitation, in these reports, is not about volume. It's about a sense that the One addressed is close. There's a third picture of Abu Musa's people that fits. Bukhari records the Prophet praising the Ash'aris, Abu Musa's tribe, because when their food ran low they gathered everything they had on one cloth and shared it out equally. They are from me, he said, and I am from them. A people known for sharing, and one of them known for a voice. Neither the food nor the voice was kept to themselves.
screen: `MIZMAR, A REED PIPE.` · `NOT DEAF, NOT ABSENT: NEAR.` · `BEAUTY IS CARE, NOT VOLUME.` · `THE ASH'ARIS SHARED THEIR FOOD.` · then, large: `A VOICE LIKE DAWUD'S.`

segments.voice: The practice: recite softly and well. Let the room go quiet around you. If you know a short surah, or even al-Fatiha, you can say it now, quietly, almost under your breath. Slowly. Give each letter its place. Don't rush the long vowels. If you don't recite, you can do the same with any words that matter to you, or simply listen to your own breathing as if it were a sound worth tending. Not loud. Close. As if speaking to someone who is near. The bell holds the time.
Abu Musa. A companion from Yemen whose recitation the Prophet compared to a pipe of the family of Dawud, and who also reported: you call on One who hears, and is near. Today's word.
Your line: a voice like Dawud's. Today, the next time you feel the urge to raise your voice to be heard, lower it instead, once. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Hudhayfah, keeper of secrets
860.hook: the keeper of secrets, who asked about harm so he could avoid it
860.howItsDone: Muslims quote Hudhayfah's words about asking of evil in order to avoid it, and scholars cite his long report in Bukhari when discussing how to hold fast during times of trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Musa, whose recitation the Prophet heard in the night. Your line was: a voice like Dawud's. When did you lower your voice instead of raising it? Day eight hundred sixty.

What brings reward? What is best? Those were the questions people brought to the Prophet. Later, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, a companion, tells his listeners how his own questions ran the other way. People used to ask the Messenger of God about the good, he says. I used to ask him about the evil, because I was afraid it would catch me. Plenty of us collect advice about what to do. Hudhayfah collected warnings. Today: Hudhayfah.
screen: `THEY ASKED ABOUT THE GOOD.` → `HE ASKED ABOUT THE EVIL.` → `AFRAID IT WOULD CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: That sentence opens a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Hudhayfah goes on to describe a conversation with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He asks: we were in ignorance and harm, and God brought us this good. Will there be harm after this good? Yes, the Prophet says. And after that harm, good again? Yes, but with some smoke in it, some haze. The questions keep going, Hudhayfah pressing for the next turn and the next, until he asks the practical one: and if that time reaches me, what do you command me to do? The point of all the asking was not gloom. It was a plan. Find out where the road gets dangerous so you can walk around it. His fellow companions noticed something else about him. In Bukhari, Abu al-Darda refers to Hudhayfah as the one among them who holds the secret that no one else knows. Tradition says the Prophet had told him things he told no one else, including who among the people of Medina were hypocrites, and that Hudhayfah kept it. Some reports say even Umar would ask him, worried, whether his own name was on that list, and that Hudhayfah would only say no to him, and name no one else. Those details come from later reports, not from Bukhari. Put the two together. The man who asked about harm was also the man trusted with hard knowledge, and he didn't spend it on gossip. Knowing where the danger was did not make him suspicious of everyone. It made him careful with himself, and quiet about others: honest about the dark, and discreet with what he knew.
screen: `WILL THERE BE HARM AFTER THIS?` · `GOOD AGAIN, BUT WITH HAZE.` · `WHAT DO YOU COMMAND ME TO DO?` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SECRET.` · then, large: `ASK ABOUT THE HARM.`

segments.voice: The practice: know your own weak spot. Close your eyes if that helps, and breathe slowly. Ask yourself Hudhayfah's question, pointed inward. Where does harm usually catch me? A certain hour of the night. A certain app. A certain conversation that always turns sour. Anger when I'm hungry. Don't scold yourself. Just name it, the way you'd mark a pothole on your street. Breathe in, and see it clearly. Breathe out, and think of one small way to walk around it this week. If you pray, you can ask for protection from it. This one stays between you and God, or you and yourself. The bell holds the time.
Hudhayfah. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, the companion who asked the Prophet about harm so he could avoid it, remembered as the keeper of secrets. Today's word.
Your line: ask about the harm. Today, when you meet the weak spot you named, take the detour you planned, once. Day eight hundred sixty.

861.title: Salim, Mu'adh and the others
861.hook: four the Prophet ﷺ named as teachers of the Qur'an: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh and Ubayy
861.howItsDone: Muslims learn to recite the Qur'an from a teacher face to face, and chains of recitation are traced back through companions such as Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hudhayfah, who asked about harm so he could avoid it. Your line was: ask about the harm. Did you take the detour you planned? Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A short list. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once named the people to go to if you wanted to learn the Qur'an. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Salim, the freed man of Abu Hudhayfah. Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Three of those names have had a day of their own on this path already. One hasn't. And he's the one who, on paper, didn't belong: a man who had once been owned, whose name in the hadith is tied to someone else's. Today: Salim.
screen: `LEARN THE QUR'AN FROM FOUR.` → `THREE YOU'VE MET.` → `ONE YOU HAVEN'T.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr: learn the Qur'an from four. Ibn Mas'ud, Salim the mawla of Abu Hudhayfah, Ubayy and Mu'adh. Look at who made the list. Alongside the other three stands Salim, whose title is mawla, a word that here means a freed man still linked to the household that freed him. Tradition says Abu Hudhayfah took him in as a son. In the hadith, his name doesn't stand alone. And the Prophet sent people to him anyway. Bukhari also records what happened at Quba, before the Prophet himself reached Medina. When the first emigrants arrived, Salim led them in prayer, and the report gives the reason: he knew the most Qur'an of them. Not the best family. Not the most wealth. The most Qur'an. So the men who had left Mecca with their reputations stood behind a freed man, because of what he carried in his memory. The biographies add that Salim was later killed at the battle of Yamamah, carrying the emigrants' banner; that comes from them, not from Bukhari. What the hadith gives us for certain is the list, and the list is a kind of permission. It tells anyone who wants to learn: go to the ones who know, whoever they are. And it tells anyone who teaches, whatever their past: what you carry matters more than the name you were given. This closes a week of companions. Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd and the throne, Uways and his mother, the Ansar, Abu Musa's voice, Hudhayfah's questions, and now Salim at the front of the line in Quba.
screen: `LEARN THE QUR'AN FROM FOUR.` · `SALIM, THE FREED MAN.` · `HE LED THE PRAYER AT QUBA.` · `WHAT YOU CARRY, NOT YOUR NAME.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM THESE FOUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank your Qur'an teacher. Rest your hands, and take a few unhurried breaths. Bring to mind whoever taught you to read the Qur'an, or taught you al-Fatiha, or the prayer, or the first Arabic letters. A parent. A teacher at the mosque. A friend. An app voice, even. If you never had one, think of whoever first taught you something you still use every day. Breathe in, and see them clearly. Breathe out, and thank them in your mind. If you pray, you can ask good for them. The bell holds the time.
Salim. Salim the freed man of Abu Hudhayfah, named by the Prophet among four to learn the Qur'an from, who led the first emigrants in prayer at Quba. Today's word.
Your line: learn from these four. Today, send a thank-you to someone who taught you, in a message, a call, or a prayer. Day eight hundred sixty-one.
